THE N. Y. TRIBUNE.
WASHINGTON, July 11, 1863.


MOVEMENTS OF GEN. MCDOWELL.
The Court Of Inquiry at St. Louis having closed its business, Gen. McDowell has arrived in Washington. He is to proceed to New-York to organize an important Board for the retiring of army officers.


GEN. SICKLES.


Gen. Sickles is much improved, and his surgeon now says there is no doubt of his final recovery.


NEGROES FOR TEAMSTERS.
Gen. Banks has ordered that hereafter none but negroes shall be employed as Government teamsters in the Department of the Gulf.


CHAPLAINS' DUTIES TO DECEASED SOLDIERS.
Gen. Foster has ordered that all soldiers lying in the hospitals of the Department of North Carolina shall have the privilege of calling upon any chaplain of whatever religious denomination. In case of the death of a soldier the chaplain is instructed to communicate with his friends and relations by letter giving such details of his last moments, and expressed wishes as may tend to assure them that he has been properly cared for, and may afford them comfort in their loss.


COLLISION OF RAILROAD TRAINS—SOLDIERS INJURED.


A special train on the Baltimore and Washington Railroad, filled with soldiers, collided this morning near the Relay House with a special freight train, and 50 soldiers belonging to the 115th and 14th New York Regiments injured by the collision; one has since died. The injured men are all now at Carver Hospital.


TRANSFERRED.


Lieut. Thos. Williams, jr., has been relieved from Gen. McDowell's staff and ordered to take command in the 5th U. S. Artillery.


CHANGE IN THE FRAMING REGULATIONS.
The following circular has been issued:


POST-OFFICE DEPARTMENT, APPOINTMENT OFFICE.


WASHINGTON, July 11, 1863.
SIR—The fifth subdivision of instruction under the Post Office Law is hereby amended, by striking out the word and inserting the following before the subclause:
"seed cuttings and clones to be limited to thirty ounces." By order of the General.


ALEXANDER W. RANDALL,
First Assistant Postmaster General.


CONFISCATION.


Proceedings under the Confiscation Act have been commenced in Alexandria, Va., with reference to real estate belonging to persons now said to be in the Rebel service.


THE RAILROAD ACCIDENT.
An accident occurred very early this morning on the Washington branch of the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad, about four miles this side of Annapolis Junction. One of the trains stopped on the main track for water, but this fact did not become known to the engineer of the second train, both from this city, in time to prevent it from running into the former. The crash was terrible. The passengers were principally troops. Thirty or forty, including sixteen officers, were wounded, some of them seriously, if not fatally. The sufferers were brought back to Washington in the 11 o'clock train.

The TWO CANDIDATES.

On Wednesday, the 7th of Oct, the Convention of the Unconditional Union party of Delaware assembled at Dover, and nominated the Hon. Nathaniel B. Smithers for their Representative to Congress. On the following day, the Convention of the Copperhead party also met at Dover, and nominated for their Representative to Congress, the Ex Hon Charles Brown, of Philadelphia notoriety.

These men are fit representatives of their respective parties. Mr. Smithers needs no eulogy to Delawareans, for they know him, and to know is but to eulogize; for the past nineteen years he has thoroughly identified himself with Delaware politics, and there has been during that period but few measures for Delaware's welfare, that has not felt the impress of his intellect; but, though he has participated in all the questions of his time, he stands before the people of Delaware to-day, unblemished, and without a single spot or stain, to sully his fair name. His distinguishing characteristics, from most politicians, are purity of motives, honesty of purpose, impartiality in the search of truth, utter regardlessness of self, scouring all personal ambition, thinking only of principle, acting only from principle, in short, possessing all the qualities which stamp him as one of those men who elevate politics from thimble rigging tricks, low intriguing or mere managing, onto which such men as Brown would degrade to the greatest science of ifs. Mr. Smithers is preeminently a leader—a leader, in the true sense of the word—not one who is satisfied to drift along with the course of events, but one who takes them by the forelock, and makes them follow him—not one who is shaped by events, but one who shapes them—not one who inquires whether principle is popular but one who asks whether it is right, and when convinced of its rightfulness he is immovable, and will maintain it against all odds; and here may say, that Mr. Smithers has sometimes opposed the wish of the majority of the people, but only, because he preferred their welfare to their wish. If you would think of Mr. Smithers as lawyer, consult the records of the courts and you will find ample evidence of his ability; or as a speaker, read his speeches, and you will find them all consisting of sound reason, able argument, veridical eloquence and an earnestness that amounts to conviction; or, as public man, ask his party the part he has taken in shaping its policy.

Or, if you would know him as a private citizen, ask his neighbors, and they will answer character unimpeachable; from all these sources of information, you can come to but one conclusion, namely, that Mr. Smithers is a valuable citizen, an able lawyer, a bold thinker, an earnest speaker, and leader of his party. As a personal friend of Mr. Smithers, I would have preferred an opponent more worthy of his steel, but a member of the Union Party who feels the importance of success, and wishes to repose in it, false security, hail with joy Mr. Brown's nomination, for if one thinks he can ensure the success of our candidate, it was for the copperheads to nominate such a man as Charlie Brown. Brown is a new name in Delaware politics, though I believe that gentleman was not exactly imported for this nomination, as he removed from Philadelphia to Dover about three years ago, where he has been singularly silent, not having, to my knowledge, indulged in speech-making, the favorite occupation of such CASEY people. When Mr. Brown comes to let him represent them in Congress, (which is a very modest request for him to make,) they will not only be very happy to, but will have the right to ask him, what claims he has upon them for their votes, or why they should wish him to represent them in Congress. Whatever he may assign as his claims for the confidence of the people of Delaware, he certainly cannot base any of them on their gratitude for past services; since, during the short time he has honored our State with his presence, he has neither acquired local fame nor local notoriety; national reputation would be a sufficient claim, but that also the gentleman is lamentably wanting. Or if he has any, I must confess myself in blissful ignorance of it. Mr. Brown represented, or mis-represented, I know not which, one of the districts of Philadelphia, once or more in Congress, where he was chiefly distinguished in making windy speeches, and always having an eye upon the main chance, which probably accounts for his desire to again occupy his coveted seat. Mr. Brown also condescended to be Collector of the Port of Philadelphia during Pierce's administration, where he became so careless in his old tricks, that the ugly matter of them 1870 dollars stared him in the face. When Mr. Brown retired from office, he was pronounced by those who owned and used him, as not fit for further service, owing to his not being able to explain satisfactorily, to certain gentlemen, the mystery of them 1870 dollars, and always being perennially silent on that subject; but I do not wish to be considered as blaming the gentleman for his silence, for he may have good reasons for being silent, for instance, he may have nothing to say. Mr. Brown is the cast of broken-down, Philadelphia politician, an old party hack, who, according to a Philadelphia paper, could not have obtained the nomination of Constable in his ward; hence, his emigration to Delaware, where under copperhead patronage, he insults the intelligence of the people of Delaware, by asking them for their votes, as representative to Congress. People of Delaware, who have such mysteries as them 1870 dollars to explain, Charles Brown is a fit representative, but as to those who have no such mysteries, I ask, can Charles Brown, who has, be your suitable representative? If not, then proclaim your indignation at the ballot box. Giving rousing minority for Smithers and Union. I have not compared these men, there is no comparison between them; I have only spoken of them as they are, and have been. At my next I shall speak of them in their relation to the issues of the hour. And until then,

A. OBSERVER.

MAN'S inhumanity to man makes countless thousands mourn!

It is true of this as well as of past generations. It is true at home and abroad. Especially is it true in North Carolina—in the county of Ason.

Dear Mr. Editor, since I last wrote you, I have seen sights, have seen sorrowful and suffering women and children—suffering for bread—children crying for bread, and mothers crying because they had no bread to give them. Hear the testimony of one of these mothers—

"For days, I had been on the lookout for bread, with what little money I had, and nowhere could I find corn to sell. This one had corn to sell, and that one had no corn to sell. What shall I do? Trust in God. My aged mother started early in the morning to mill, some four or five miles away, on foot, in the hope of getting a little for we had none to give the children. As the day wore away, my heart was heavy with grief.

'Mother, has grandmother come from mill? I want some bread.'

'No, dear child, grandmother has not come yet.'

'My child wants bread, what shall I do?' The sun is high in the heavens. It is getting late. My soul was sorrowful. My eyes were full of tears. I prayed to God for bread. What shall I do for my hungry children? I raised my eyes and saw a stranger approaching the house, a cart close behind him.

'Who lives here, ma'am?'

'Mrs. S. lives here.'

'Have you any bread for your children?'

'No, sir—but mother has gone to see if she can get some at the MILL.'

'Have your children had anything to eat to-day?'

'N-o, n-o, s-i-r.'

'Here is meal and corn for YOU, ma'am.'

How I did feel! 'Here is meal for you.' Relief had come! I could now give my hungry children bread. Trust in God, for He is merciful, and thank His holy name, that there are some who are ready to help the needy soldier's family.

'What shall I pay you? I have little money.'

'Never mind the money now, ma'am. Buy what you need with the money. Make some bread, and feed your children. May God bless you and your children. Good bye.'

Now, sir, this is no "unreal mockery." It is stubborn fact. It occurred as stated and I witnessed it. True, the distress stated found relief. They had a little money—but what is money good for, if it will not purchase the means of subsistence? If it will not buy bread? Confederate notes, county scrip, and gold and silver are worth less in such a state of society as we have. Those who have grain won't sell it, won't they? A little longer, and the cup of the extortionist, now full, will run over—but not one drop of its bitterness will be wasted—or they shall drink it to the dregs. God rules, and He is just. Let them look to it, and mend their ways, soon there will be nothing for them, but "terrible looking for of Judgment to come, and fiery indignation which shall devour the adversaries" of God and the people. What is the meaning of the words, "Inasmuch as ye did it not unto the least of these, my BRETHREN, ye did it not unto me!" MARTHA Ann.

Sir: I am instructed by the President of the Confederate States of America to inform you that this Government has received a despatch from Flag Officer Ingraham relating the naval forces of the Confederacy off the coast of South Carolina, stating that the blockade in the bay of Charleston has been broken by the complete dispersion and disappearance of the blockading squad, consequent to a successful attack made on it by the ironclad steamers commanded by Flag Officer Ingraham. How to keep a Hotel.

A New Orleans paper of old date contains the following excellent story which may as well be handed out a laugh catcher in these times of gloom:

Several weeks ago two well known gentlemen of this city went travelling for the benefit of their health, and concluded to try the famous Hot Springs of old "Rockensack." There being neither river, rail-road, nor canal to take a body to the Springs, our travellers hired horses at their point of debarkation, to ride in that manner to their destination. They unluckily did not follow the right road, or else there was no right road to follow at any rate they got lost, and after fatiguing days' ride through barren and inhospitable wilderness, they came to a neat little building standing alone in the woods with farming appendages around. Our travellers halted and hallooed. A great, tall, raw boated giant of fellow stepped out.

"Well, gentlemen, I recken we kim," said the big one, "and welkim to boot. This is a hotel."

The travellers, although they did not like the cut of the landlord's jib, dismounted, were relieved of their horses, and were soon regaling themselves over good country supper of corn dodgers, bacon, milk, fried chickens and coffee. It was regular country supper, but with their whetted appetites our invalids enjoyed it amazingly.

After supper the gigantic landlord sat on the porch with them talking, laughing, cracking jokes, and treating occasionally to some good old rye, of which he appeared to have plentiful stock. The invalids set him down for regular "brick," and were still better pleased when lighted at last to nice soft feather beds, with the whitest and sweetest of sheets.

"I tell you what it is, Bill," said Tom, as they were sinking slowly into the embrace of Slumber, "this fellow keeps a nice place, if it is out here in the woods."

"That's fact," replied Bill, "and I suppose its cheap place, too; but I like it, and I'm willing to pay the full city figure on it."

Next morning our travellers were aroused by their ugly but affable landlord, and regaled with a breakfast, if possible, still more appetising than the last night's supper had been. The horses were brought around and it was evident that they too had been well cared for. One of the travelers pulled out his wallet, and said to the big entertainer:

"Well, Landlord, you keep first rate little hotel out here better than we expected to find. We are much pleased with it, and now want to know what the damage is."

The landlord drew himself up, and putting on very solemn look, said: "Gentlemen, am pleased to hear yer satisfied. The bill is two hundred and seventy five dollars."

"How much do you say, sir?" asked the travellers, both startled.

The big one drawing himself up little higher, and looking still more solemn, replied, distinctly and emphatically, "TWO hundred and seventy five dollars, gentlemen."

"Do I hear you alright, sir? Do you really mean to charge us two hundred and seventy-five dollars for two meals, and lodging, and horse feed?"

"Gentlemen," said the landlord, with the most alarming sangfroid, "that's no mistake. Two hundred and seventy-five dollars is the bill."

The invalids got scared. They did not feel strong enough to fight and if they had, could never have hoped to make anything out of the ungainly giant who stood so composedly before them. Without saying another word the traveller with the wallet it and peeled its different pockets, and succeeded in handing over the full amount required. The landlord thanked his guests politely, and hoped if they should ever pass that way again, that they would give him call.

The travellers were now on their horses, and prepared, like the famous cavaliers in James novels, to resume their solitary ride. Before getting far off, however, the traveller who had to disgorge, turned in his saddle, and hailed the landlord.

"I say, landlord," he shouted, "before I go, I'd just like to ask you one question: a civil question—which YOU can't take offence at."

"Fire ahead, gentlemen," was the answer. "Ye've paid yer bill, and yer welkim to ask anything without offence."

"Well, now, in the name of heaven, did you come to charge us two hundred and seventy five dollars for one night's accommodation not worth more than five or six dollars at the outside?"

"Certainly, gentlemen, I'll tell yer, and welkim. Yer see I keep hotel and sometimes has customers and sometimes hasn't. When hasn't, I has to charge accordingly; and as you are the first customers I've had well nigh on a year, yer bill was little bigger'n it mought ha' bin. The hotel has to be KEEP up, gentlemen, and when customers is scarce, I has to charge accordingly."

"Good morning, landlord," said both, and they rode off satisfied.

They didn't go on to the Springs, however. They took the back track for the river, and returned to this city for more money, the big hotel keeper having pretty well cleaned them out. Resupplied with funds, they are now off to the Virginia Springs; being unwilling to trust themselves again among the hotels of Arkansas interior.

They declare, though, that the big landlord who fleeced them is a capital fellow—all sorts of a fellow—and knows how to keep hotel into the bargain.

A correspondent of the Cincinnati Gazette refers to the position and maneuvering of the Federal and rebel army in Tennessee as similar to the wily play of two swordsmen, and says:


The history of the Union and rebel armies in Middle Tennessee for the past two months is the history of just such a sleepless trial of vigilance and skill as that between the swordsmen. The rebels seem not to rest even for an hour. At times a series of demonstrations will commence on one of our wings, and extend entirely round to the other, as though the rebels would examine every portion of the circle within which lies the Union army, and discover, if possible, its vulnerable point. But wherever he looks he finds himself confronted by armed men, ready, if he desires, to accept his challenge and try conclusions with him. Checked in this manner, he quietly withdraws, and not a gun is fired on either side. So, too, the enemy while he is making demonstrations upon our lines, suddenly discovers that Reynolds or Wilder is threatening his own, and at once begins a series of withdrawals or counter movements to check or battle the supposed design. And thus the ceaseless movement goes on, and the observer constantly beholds bodies of troops marching and countermarching, going this way and that without any apparent object.


But by and by all this preliminary play will be over, and all Middle Tennessee will tremble with the tread of mighty hosts and the shock of contending arms. Both armies are strong and confident. The opposing generals are well aware of the magnitude of the stake for which they play. The most superficial observer can appreciate the beneficent results to the Union cause which would attend the expulsion of the enemy from East Tennessee; while the rebels universally believe as their prisoners say, as their presses indicate, and as their private letters "a large number of which I have recently read declare, that if they could only succeed in crushing Rosecrans, it would be equivalent to the triumph of the rebellion. Washington, November 11, 1863,

BIDS PROPOSALS. Bids to be received at this office

N. J. CARPENTER, ESQ, Milwaukee, Wis

SIR:—I have read with so much satisfaction your letter upon the subject of the duty OF the democratic party in the present crisis OF our national affairs, that I venture to express the hope that all may see the subject as you have so powerfully expressed it. In my judgment your manner OF disposing of the points of objection Is so clear and SO eminently adapted to the crisis that no successful reply can be made.

The south set the house on fire: you and I were lodging in its apartments, and must stand by with inaccessible indifference and see the edifice utterly destroyed or manfully try to extinguish the flames. How utterly destructive is the policy OF calling jury to try and convict the incendiary before the house is saved. Before the witnesses can be examined, the edifice will be in ashes.

We must not allow anybody to make peace, until all the States resume their original "status" under the old flag and old constitution. And whether the status OF the local institutions of the south is to be preserved or not, depends greatly on the duration of the war. All military decrees OF the president must be understood as a means to accomplish the end—a restoration of the Union as it was. The object OF the government in prosecuting the war has been officially declared in Congress. The proclamations of the president declaring the blockade of our ports, and emancipating the slaves in the insurrectionary states are only means to the end. If we keep out supplies and munitions of war by the external blockade; and if we can effectually keep an internal blockade on these states by keeping the enemy from planting, sowing and reaping supplies at home, the war must soon end. If the emancipation proclamation withdraws twenty-five or fifty thousand laborers from their fields and internal production, or from their fortifications and rifle pits, it is an active and effectual means to the desired end.

In my judgment we ought to capture as contraband OF war, every effective negro in the insurgent states that we can reach, and hold them as means of weakening the enemy and closing the war. In fact every objection made to the president's proclamation can best be settled after an honorable peace.

All ideas OF peace with the states in active rebellion are delusive at present. The lamented Douglas with prophetic judgment gave us the true idea of this war when he said "the surest road to peace is the most stupendous preparations for war;" I would urge our democratic friends from one end of the north to the other, to adopt this as their motto, and it will prove "bread cast upon the waters" to be found "after many days." Let us prove our patriotism by our works; any other course is weakness and madness as I view it.

We all want peace, but when it comes, the whole Union must come with it. We are near the hour of our final success, I firmly believe. With the capture or occupation OF Vicksburg by our forces, peace must and will speedily come.

I am with great respect,

W. A. GORMAN,

Brig Gen. U. S. Vols.

up. Fine fleece wool that could have

At about three o'clock, another Mississippi

the enemy. Anderson advancing his skirmishers drove in those of the Federals.

of Kershaw's brigade during this attack
on the enemy's right, were engaged in
holding them in check in front.

command of Generals Kelley and Grace, of
Preston's Division, reported to General
Kershaw for orders, and were assigned to a
position in rear of the Carolinians, with
Kelley on Grace's right. Soon after Gen.
eral Hindman opened with his artillery on
the right flank of the enemy, informing Ker-
shaw, however, that his attack was not
likely to succeed unless seconded by efforts
in front. General Kershaw thereupon de-

attacks of the day, that which now followed

order moved like a rolling wave, the men
animated by the thought that upon the

tiny of the day, and the future of the Con-

I hear no confirmation of the statement which I had heard, and which sent you few days since regarding the difference of opinion said to exist between Generals Thomas and Rosecrans upon the subject of holding Chattanooga. But additional facts which have obtained, some of which I will not disclose, very significant, can't but though danger comes not would be led to surmise from my former letter this subject from the movements of the enemy, much from the scarcity of provisions and forage, and that the animals are living on quarter rations and that many cannot obtain that insufficient supply. There is an order that private animals shall not be allowed to go from Stevenson to Chattanooga, and only the pack mules which carry the supplies to Chattanooga are permitted to cross the mountains. The troops have a sufficiency of the rougher rations of hard bread and pork and occasionally rations of fresh beef, flour and meal, hard tack, and what little reaches the besieged city to the hospitals.

It remains to be seen whether this scarcity of forage and provisions will drive us out of this portion of Tennessee we have paid so dearly for.

THE RAILROAD BRIDGEPORT TO CHATTANOOGA.

The opening of the railroad Bridgeport to Chattanooga must be undertaken very soon, fear matters may assume bad shape at Chattanooga. The army cannot be supplied during the winter season by the present means. I presume that an effort will be made by the Eleventh corps to cross and open this route within a short time, as the railroad bridge Bridgeport is finished. An engagement of minor importance will doubtless follow demonstrations looking towards this line; it will also be necessary to take possession of the summit of Lookout Mountain, and an engagement of greater or less dimensions may be expected there. At any rate, I declare that the railroad must be opened before winter sets in, and the army supplied by that means or the position must be evacuated.

GENERAL BURNSIDE HAS FACED BRAGG.

Whether there is any truth in the statement which I heard this morning from one of Grant's staff officers, appears Bragg intends to depend entirely on General Starvation to drive Thomas from Chattanooga. This is the effect, as a corps of Bragg's army was pushing up the valley towards London and Kingston with the purpose of attacking Burnside. This movement would flank Thomas, and a portion of Bragg's army was unexpected, and the information startling, only because I was told that Ewell is in command; it was said that Ewell was engaged in the Chickamauga fights, but this fallacy is already exposed. But of late we have been told that Ewell's corps had moved to Bragg's side, this positive statement that the commander has moved up the valley. We shall probably hear further from this story in a day or two.

INTERRUPTION OF RAILROAD COMMUNICATION.

As the telegraph has informed you, the railroad communication between this point and Stevenson's is very much interrupted. No train has left here for the South since my arrival except yesterday, which returned after having gone ten miles southward. We have the promise of a train tomorrow, but there is little probability of getting through. There is little, nothing of interest here, and certainly no other attractions which would make the place a delightful winter abode.

ESTABLISHED AT NASHVILLE.

It is stated here that, in all probability, Assistant Secretary of War Dana will make his headquarters here and establish a branch of War, in which he and Gen. McLeans will represent the administration. I also thought that Grant in person will remain here. It is believed by all that the active operations of the war are over and will be confined to preparations for active labor in the spring. The labor of organizing Thomas' army and keeping it alive are of Herculean character, and which General Thomas will not be envied.

Of late the rebels have been using torpedoes in a new manner, and to-day succeeded in blowing up the third locomotive within four days. A train was blown up near Oran to-day and entirely destroyed. The torpedo was placed on the track and under a bridge or culvert.
